section.title: Paul's Vision and Thorn
section.sectionRationale: Forced by the boasting of the false teachers to speak of himself, Paul turns at last to the one thing they cannot match, visions and revelations from the Lord. Yet he tells of being caught up to the third heaven in the third person, refuses to trade on it, and then reveals the thorn in the flesh God gave to keep him humble. The passage climbs to the Lord's own word, My grace is sufficient for you, and Paul inverts every rule of boasting: he will glory in his weakness, for that is where the power of Christ rests.
section.thesis: The gospel minister's true credential is not spiritual experience but the sufficiency of Christ's grace displayed in weakness, for the Lord perfects His power in weakness, and the servant who is weak in himself is strong in Christ.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the vision caught up to Paradise, told at arm's length; the thorn in the flesh and the threefold plea; and the Lord's answer, My grace is sufficient, so that Paul now boasts gladly in weakness.

units.label: Caught up to Paradise
units.note: visions and revelations from the Lord

verses.text: I must go on boasting. Although there is nothing to gain, I will go on to visions and revelations from the Lord.
I know a man in Christ who fourteen years ago was caught up to the third heaven. Whether it was in the body or out of it I do not know, but God knows.
And I know that this man, whether in the body or out of it I do not know, but God knows,
was caught up to Paradise. The things he heard were inexpressible, things that man is not permitted to tell.
I will boast about such a man, but I will not boast about myself, except in my weaknesses.
Even if I wanted to boast, I would not be a fool, because I would be speaking the truth. But I refrain, so no one will credit me with more than he sees in me or hears from me,

units.label: The thorn in the flesh
units.note: a messenger of Satan, and three pleas

verses.text: or because of these surpassingly great revelations. So to keep me from becoming conceited, I was given a {{skolops|thorn}} in my flesh, a messenger of Satan, to torment me.
Three times I pleaded with the Lord to take it away from me.

units.label: My grace is sufficient for you

verses.text: But He said to me, “My {{charis|grace}} is sufficient for you, for My power is {{teleo|perfected}} in weakness.” Therefore I will boast all the more gladly in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest on me.
That is why, for the sake of Christ, I delight in {{astheneia|weaknesses}}, in insults, in hardships, in persecutions, in difficulties. For when I am weak, then I am strong.

skolops.gloss: A sharp stake, splinter, or thorn. The word can mean anything from a small splinter under the skin to an impaling stake, so it conveys real and constant pain. Paul calls this thorn a messenger of Satan, yet it was given by God for a good end, to keep His servant from pride. Scripture leaves the thing itself unnamed, so that every afflicted believer may find their own trouble here.

charis.gloss: Grace, unmerited favor, the free and powerful kindness of God. Here grace is not merely pardon but sustaining strength: the Lord says His grace is sufficient, enough to carry Paul through the unremoved thorn. Grace is proved sufficient precisely where human strength runs out, so that the weakness which humbles the servant becomes the stage for God's power.

teleo.gloss: To bring to completion, to make perfect, to reach full expression. Christ's power is not merely present in weakness but perfected in it, brought to its fullest display where the servant has nothing of his own. The word overturns every worldly measure of strength: divine power comes to its goal not by removing our weakness but by working through it.

astheneia.gloss: Weakness, frailty, sickness, or lack of strength. Paul lists a whole family of weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and difficulties, in which he now delights for Christ's sake. Far from hiding his frailty, he makes it his boast, because it is the very place where the power of Christ comes to rest upon him. When I am weak, then I am strong.

basic.context: The false teachers at Corinth boasted of dazzling spiritual experiences, so Paul, forced to answer, tells of being caught up fourteen years ago to the third heaven, to Paradise, where he heard things too holy to repeat. But he tells it in the third person and refuses to trade on it. Instead he speaks of a thorn in the flesh, a painful trouble God gave to keep him humble. Three times he begged for it to go, and the Lord answered, My grace is sufficient for you. So Paul now boasts not in his visions but in his weakness.
basic.hermeneutics: Read the vision and the thorn together, for they are two halves of one point. The revelation could have puffed Paul up; the thorn keeps him low; and the Lord's word makes weakness itself the place of power. The passage is not first about mystical experience but about how God keeps and uses His servants. The climax is the Lord's saying in verse 9, which reframes the whole boast.
basic.originalLanguages: The trouble is a skolops, a stake or thorn, real and constant pain, left deliberately unnamed. Against it stands the Lord's charis, His grace, which is sufficient. His power is not merely shown but teleo, perfected, brought to its fullest, in weakness. So Paul glories in astheneia, weakness, for there Christ's strength rests on him.
basic.typology: Paul's pattern of strength through weakness follows the shape of the cross itself, where Christ was crucified in weakness yet lives by God's power. As Israel's deliverance often came when they were fewest and weakest, so the apostle's power is made perfect where he is least. The unremoved thorn, borne in trust, echoes every sufferer whom God sustains rather than spares.
basic.christ: The grace that is sufficient is the grace of Christ, and the power that rests on Paul is the power of Christ. The Lord who answers the threefold plea is Jesus, who Himself prayed three times in Gethsemane and was answered not by removal but by strength to obey. Christ is the pattern and the source: crucified in weakness, raised in power, He makes His servant strong in his weakness.
basic.god: God is sovereign even over the messenger of Satan, bending the enemy's torment to His own gracious purpose of humbling and keeping His servant. He is the God who gives grace rather than always removing the trouble, and whose power is displayed most brightly against the backdrop of human frailty. He will not share His glory, so He works where no flesh can boast.
basic.crossReferences: Philippians 4 says God's strength is sufficient for all things through Christ. 2 Corinthians 4 speaks of treasure in jars of clay so the power may be God's. Isaiah 40 promises strength to the weak and weary who wait on the Lord.
basic.oneStory: From the exodus to the cross, God has saved through weakness so that no one can boast before Him. Here that pattern becomes personal: the great apostle is kept low by a thorn and told that grace is enough. The whole Bible moves toward the crucified and risen Christ, whose power is perfected in weakness and rests on all who are weak in themselves but strong in Him.

context.literary:
This passage is the high point of the fool's speech, and it is built as a rise and a fall. Verses 1 to 6 climb: Paul announces that he must go on boasting, moves to 'visions and revelations from the Lord,' and describes a journey to the third heaven and Paradise. The narrative is told twice, in verses 2 to 3 and 3 to 4, with the same refrain, 'whether in the body or out of it I do not know, but God knows.' The repetition is a kind of liturgy of unknowing, and it forces the reader to slow down.

Then verse 7 turns. The structure of the Greek sentence is delicate, and the BSB footnote notes that some translators end the previous paragraph after verse 6 and begin verse 7 with 'So to keep me from becoming conceited because of these surpassingly great revelations.' Either way, the thought is that the revelations create a danger, and the danger is answered by a gift. A twice repeated clause in verse 7 gives the reason, 'to keep me from becoming conceited.' The passage that began in a heavenly place ends in a bruising, earthbound pain.

Verses 8 to 10 are a small prayer narrative: a threefold plea, a divine answer in direct speech, and a response. The Lord's words are the one place in the letter where Christ is heard speaking to Paul, and they sit at the exact centre of the fool's speech. Everything before this prepares for them and everything after depends on them.

The third person style matters. Paul says 'I know a man in Christ,' as though he were reporting about someone else, and only in verse 7 does he step back into the first person. He is not hiding; he is putting a distance between himself and the experience so as to refuse its use as a credential. In verse 6 he says that even if he wished to boast about it he would not be a fool, because he would be telling the truth, but he declines so that no one will credit him with more than he sees in him or hears from him. The structure is therefore an argument: the experiences were real, he will not use them, and the only thing he will boast in is what he can show the churches in plain sight, his weakness.
context.historical:
The Corinthians lived in a religious culture that prized ecstasy. Pagan temples around them offered experiences of the divine through ritual, and Jewish apocalyptic writing of the period described heavenly journeys in elaborate detail. The rivals appear to have claimed visions as part of their authority. A teacher who could point to a heavenly ascent could claim a higher standing than one who could not.

Paul's account fits a Jewish tradition of heavenly ascent. Some Jewish writings described several heavens, with different numbers, and the third heaven in Paul's account is the place of God's own presence, since he equates it with Paradise. In Jewish thought, Paradise was the garden of God, the place of the righteous, and the word is used by Jesus in Luke 23:43 for where the repentant criminal would be with Him that day. The word reappears in Revelation 2:7, where the tree of life stands in the Paradise of God. For Paul, being caught up to Paradise means entering the very presence of God.

The date matters. Writing about AD 55 or 56, Paul says the event took place fourteen years earlier, which puts it around AD 41 or 42. That is before his famous missionary journeys and during the years when he was in Tarsus and Syria, Acts 9:30 and 11:25. He has kept it to himself for fourteen years. This is an example of reticence in a culture of display.

The Old Testament knows the cost of seeing. Moses was told that no one can see God's face and live, Exodus 33:20. Daniel's strength left him after his vision, Daniel 10:8, and John fell at the feet of the risen Lord like a dead man, Revelation 1:17. Isaiah, in the temple, cried out that he was ruined, Isaiah 6. The pattern in Scripture is that great revelation is followed by weakness or humbling, not self-confidence. Paul's thorn fits that pattern, and the Corinthians, who valued spiritual experience as proof of status, are being given a lesson from their own tradition.
context.canonical:
The passage draws on a long line of Scripture about the cost and the safeguard of seeing God. Isaiah saw the Lord seated on a throne and said he was undone, Isaiah 6:1 and 6:5. Ezekiel saw visions of God by the River Kebar, Ezekiel 1:1, and fell on his face. Moses alone spoke with God face to face, Numbers 12:6 to 8. Paul's journey belongs in this company, but his response is to hold back and not to publish.

The thorn has an Old Testament background in the language of Numbers 33:55, where the nations left in the land would be 'barbs in your eyes and thorns in your sides,' and Ezekiel 28:24, where Israel will no longer face 'a pricking brier or a painful thorn.' In both texts thorns are agents of harassment, and in the Greek Old Testament Numbers 33:55 uses the same noun, skolops, that Paul uses here. This is one reason many readers think of personal opponents, though it does not settle the matter.

The pattern of a satanic agent allowed to act within God's limits recalls Job 2:6, where Satan is permitted to touch Job under strict limits, and Luke 22:31 to 32, where Satan asked to sift Simon like wheat and Jesus prayed that his faith would not fail. In each case the enemy is on a leash.

The Lord's answer takes up the language of grace that runs through the whole Bible. The promise of strength to the weak is in Isaiah 40:29, and the contest between human strength and God's in 1 Corinthians 1:25 to 27. In 2 Corinthians 13:4 Paul says that Christ was crucified in weakness and lives by God's power. In Hebrews 4:15 to 16 we have a high priest who sympathises with our weaknesses and a throne of grace where we find help in time of need. And in Philippians 4:13 the same Paul says he can do all things through Christ who gives him strength, a verse that needs this passage beside it to be read rightly.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul meant the Corinthians to see that his refusal to boast of his visions was a choice, not an absence. He had more to boast of than his rivals; he simply would not. In saying so he exposes the weakness of their method, since a gift from God that tempts to pride is a hazardous thing and must be handled with care.

He also meant them to hear the thorn as a gift. The passive in verse 7, 'was given,' places God behind it, and the purpose clause says why: to keep him from becoming conceited. The suffering is a form of divine care, and what looks like a disadvantage is the thing that keeps him close to Christ.

Above all, he meant them to hear the Lord's answer as a rule for all of ministry. The one who is strong in himself has no need of grace; the one who is weak has all of it. The conclusion, 'when I am weak, then I am strong,' is not a slogan but a description of how the Lord works, and it turns the Corinthians' admiration of strength upside down. If they want a mark of true apostleship, here it is: an apostle who, having asked three times for relief, was told no and gave thanks.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage records one man's experience and one prayer that was answered by a refusal. It does not command believers to refuse healing, to avoid asking God to remove hardship, or to treat every illness as a thorn from God. Paul himself asked, and asked again. Prayer for deliverance is right and is the pattern here.

It also does not describe a general rule about visions. Paul does not say believers should seek heavenly experiences or expect them, and he does not use his own to settle any question of doctrine. What he heard he was not permitted to repeat, verse 4. This is a restraint, and it guards the gospel from being replaced by private revelation.

What carries forward is the Lord's answer, because it is addressed to Paul but speaks of a principle: grace is enough and power is perfected in weakness. Believers who live with an unremoved difficulty, whether pain, loss or limitation, are not told that it is good in itself, but that Christ's grace meets them in it. The right response is not resignation but trust, joined to the freedom to pray, and the willingness to receive help from Christ and from one another.

debates.question: What was the thorn in the flesh?

views.label: A physical illness or disability
views.case: Some point to Galatians 4:13 to 15, where Paul says that an illness was the reason he first preached to the Galatians and that they would have torn out their eyes for him, and conclude that it was a problem with his eyes or some other persistent bodily ailment. Others suggest a recurring condition such as fever or headaches. The word 'flesh' in verse 7 favours a bodily affliction, and the verb 'torment' suggests pain.

views.label: Opponents or persecution
views.case: Because 'messenger of Satan' can mean a human agent, and because Numbers 33:55 and Ezekiel 28:24 use thorns for enemies, many readers think the thorn was a person or a group, perhaps the opposition that dogged him through his ministry. The word 'messenger' is the same as 'angel,' used for a person in some contexts. The surrounding chapters are about enemies in the church.

views.label: A spiritual or emotional trial
views.case: Some in the church's history, including some of the Reformers, thought the thorn was temptation or inner anguish. The text does not tell us, and the lack of a name may be deliberate.

debates.bearing: The text does not name it, and its silence makes the Lord's answer available to every kind of sufferer. If Paul had said it was a headache, only people with headaches would hear the promise. Since he does not, it speaks to sickness, opposition, temptation and grief alike. What matters is the three part pattern: the trouble, the plea, and the answer.

debates.question: What did Paul experience, and was it Paul himself?

views.label: Paul himself, in a real heavenly journey
views.case: Verse 7 speaks of 'these surpassingly great revelations,' and the thorn was given to keep him from pride about them, so the man in Christ is Paul. The passage treats the experience as true. It was an actual event, and Paul was unsure whether his body went with him, which is a sign of how overwhelming it was.

views.label: A representative or another person
views.case: A few have suggested another person, since Paul speaks of 'such a man' in the third person, but there is no sign of another figure in the passage, and verse 7 makes the link to Paul himself explicit.

debates.bearing: The first view is held by nearly every reader. The passage does not turn on the question; it turns on the way Paul refuses to use the experience. Whether or not the heavens have levels, Paradise is real and the vision was real, and what it produced in Paul was reticence, not boasting.

study.originalLanguages:
The verb that runs the first paragraph is harpazo, 'caught up,' a word of force that means to seize or snatch. It is used of Philip being carried off by the Spirit in Acts 8:39, of the child taken up to God in Revelation 12:5, and of believers 'caught up together' to meet the Lord in 1 Thessalonians 4:17. Paul uses the passive, so he is the one acted on and not the actor. He does not say he went; he says he was taken. And the word 'Paradise,' paradeisos, comes from a Persian loan word for an enclosed garden, and the Greek Old Testament uses it for the garden of Eden, so the term suggests a restored Eden.

What Paul heard was 'too sacred for words,' arrheta rhemata, 'unspeakable words.' The adjective carries a double sense, things that cannot be told and things that may not be told, and Paul adds that a man is not permitted to tell them, using a form of the verb for 'it is permitted.' Whatever the content, the effect is silence.

The thorn is a skolops, a stake or sharp point, in the Greek Old Testament used in Numbers 33:55 of the thorns in Israel's sides. The BSB renders it 'thorn,' but the noun can also mean a stake, a point driven in. The statement 'was given,' edothe, is the so called divine passive, a way of speaking of God's action without naming Him. At the same time the thorn is 'a messenger of Satan,' angelos Satana. The text keeps both: given by God, delivered by Satan. And the verb 'to torment,' kolaphizo, means to strike with the fist, and it is used of Jesus being struck in Matthew 26:67 and of Paul's own treatment in 1 Corinthians 4:11. The tense is present, which suggests a repeated or continuing buffeting, not a single blow.

The purpose clause in verse 7 uses the verb hyperairomai, to lift oneself up, twice. The point is the danger of the heights: the 'surpassingly great' revelations could lift him, so the thorn pulls him down. The double use is an echo, and it makes the thorn a precise remedy.

In verse 8 'pleaded' is parakaleo, the same verb that, as 'comfort,' fills 2 Corinthians 1:3 to 7 and is there used of God who comforts. Paul asks the Lord to take the trouble away, and the Lord does not remove it but comforts and strengthens. Here the great theme of the whole letter is turned back on the writer. And 'three times' is the number of Gethsemane, Matthew 26:44, though Paul does not point out the echo.

The Lord's answer is carefully worded. 'He said to me' is in the perfect tense in Greek, eireken, which means that the word was spoken and still stands. 'Is sufficient,' arkei, is in the present, so it is a standing sufficiency. The word 'power,' dynamis, is 'perfected,' teleitai, present passive of teleo, brought to completion. And in verse 9, 'rest on me' is episkenoo, built on skene, a tent, a word that carries the idea of pitching a tent over someone, and recalls the Word who 'made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14. In verse 10 'I delight,' eudokeo, is the verb used of the Father's pleasure in the Son in Matthew 3:17. Paul does not merely endure weakness; he is content with it, because it is the place where Christ's presence is.

typology.type: The heavenly vision and the cost of seeing, Isaiah 6:1 to 5
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah saw the Lord on a throne, and the sight undid him, until a coal from the altar cleansed his lips. Paul was taken further, into Paradise itself, and the sight left him with a wound to keep him low. The correspondence is that the closer a servant comes to God's glory, the more he is made aware of his own weakness. The escalation in Christ is that He is the glory, and in Him we see the Father's face, John 1:14. The type falls short in that Isaiah's cleansing was ritual and temporary, while Paul's thorn is borne alongside a grace that never lapses.

typology.type: The thorn left in the land, Numbers 33:55
typology.fulfillment: The nations left in the land would be thorns in Israel's sides, a lasting harassment that tested whether they would trust the LORD. Paul's thorn is not a sign of disobedience but is likewise something left in place. The correspondence is of an enduring irritant that keeps God's people dependent. In Christ, the One who had no thorn of sin, we see the pattern turned: He wore a crown of thorns, Matthew 27:29, and bore the curse so that thorns would be removed in the end. The type falls short because Paul's thorn is given for his good, while Israel's thorns came from disobedience.

typology.type: Gethsemane and the unremoved cup, Matthew 26:39 to 44
typology.fulfillment: Jesus prayed three times that the cup might pass if it were possible, and the Father did not take it away but strengthened Him to drink it. Paul's three pleas and the Lord's refusal follow the same shape: the request is honest, the answer is not removal, and the servant is held by grace. The escalation is that His cup was the cup of wrath for sin, and His obedience made it possible for any later suffering to be borne in grace. The type falls short because Paul's thorn is a discipline for pride, not a bearing of sin, and Paul's endurance does not save anyone.

Gideon's army was cut down so that Israel could not say that their own hand had saved them. The principle that God arranges weakness so that the power is plainly His runs through the Old Testament. Paul's boast that the power of Christ rests on him in weakness repeats it. The fulfilment in Christ is that the cross is the extreme case: the apparent defeat of God's Son is the victory, and all boasting is excluded, 1 Corinthians 1:27 to 29. The type falls short in that Gideon's weakness led to a military triumph, while the cross leads to a triumph over sin and death.

study.christ:
This passage leads to Christ by the voice that speaks in it. The one who answers Paul's plea is 'the Lord,' and the power that rests on Paul is 'the power of Christ.' The two titles show that the Lord who gave the word is Jesus, and the passage presents Him as the one who hears prayer, who rules over the enemy's messenger, and who defines what grace is. The sentence 'My grace is sufficient for you' is spoken by Christ in the first person, and it is the one place in this letter where the risen Lord's own words to Paul are quoted. The sufficiency is not found in a technique or an experience but in a person.

It leads to Christ by pattern. Paul's three pleas recall the three prayers in Gethsemane, where Jesus asked that the cup pass from Him if it were possible, Matthew 26:39 to 44. The Father did not remove it. He strengthened His Son to drink it, and out of that obedience came the salvation of the world. Paul's thorn is not the cup, but he learns to take his own cup in the same spirit, with prayer and with acceptance. 'Crucified in weakness, yet He lives by God's power,' says 2 Corinthians 13:4, and the sentence 'when I am weak, then I am strong' is a restatement of the resurrection pattern in the life of the believer.

It leads to Christ by sympathy. Hebrews 4:15 to 16 says we have a high priest who can sympathise with our weaknesses, and who was tempted in every way yet without sin, so that we can approach the throne of grace with confidence. The Lord who answers Paul does not speak from a distance. He has known weakness from inside, and His refusal to remove the thorn is not indifference.

It leads to Christ by dwelling. The verb 'rest on me' in verse 9 is built from the word for a tent, and recalls the Word who became flesh and 'made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14. The Christ whose glory filled the tabernacle now pitches His tent over His servant, so that the weak man becomes the place where Christ's presence is seen.

And it leads to Christ by contrast with the visions. Paul was taken to Paradise, and Jesus had promised Paradise to the thief on the cross, Luke 23:43. The place of the vision is the place where the crucified Lord is. The glory that Paul glimpsed is the glory of the one who went to the cross, and it cannot be separated from it.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The passage does not say that Christ withholds healing from His people or that suffering is always His will. It records one case and the principle behind it. Christ's answer here is not the only answer He gives, but it is always an answer that holds His grace in front of the sufferer, and it shows that He is both Lord of the thorn and the one who gives strength to bear it.
study.god:
The God of this passage is a God who gives and who withholds, and who is good in both. The visions are His gift; the thorn is His gift too, as the passive 'was given' implies. Paul does not feel that he has lost the Lord's favour because the thorn remains. He has received a better thing than relief, which is the promise of grace that is enough.

God is sovereign over the enemy's work. The thorn is called a messenger of Satan, and yet it was given for a purpose that is God's own: to keep Paul from conceit. The same pattern appears in Job 2:6, where Satan acts only within a limit set by the LORD, and in Luke 22:31 to 32, where Satan asks permission to sift Peter and Jesus prays that his faith will not fail. The Bible does not say that Satan and God are equal and opposite. It shows that the enemy's most hostile actions are turned to serve God's gracious ends. The one thing God will not do is share the credit, and so He works where no flesh can boast.

God answers prayer, though not always as we ask. Paul prays three times, and the answer is no, but it is a spoken no with a reason, a promise and a presence. This is a God who listens and who speaks back. The refusal is not silence. In the language of 2 Corinthians 1:3 to 5, He is the God of all comfort, and He comforts here by giving something better than removal.

He is the God whose power is shown in weakness. 'My power is perfected in weakness' is a statement about the divine character, not just about Paul. The Old Testament says the LORD gives power to the faint, Isaiah 40:29, and Psalm 73:26 says that when flesh and heart fail, God is the strength of the heart. The weaker the instrument, the clearer the credit goes to the one who works through it, and Ephesians 3:20 says He is able to do far more than we ask or imagine according to the power at work within us.

He is a God who keeps His servants humble for their good. The risk of pride is real, and God takes it seriously enough to wound those He loves in order to protect them. This is a hard saying, and it should be stated with care: not every pain is a safeguard, but this one was, and the passage invites us to consider that some of the limitations we resent may be doing the same work.

For worship, the passage teaches us to bring requests honestly and to hear the answer as grace. It teaches us to say with Paul that we delight in what we would not have chosen, because the Lord is in it. And it teaches us to see in our own weakness, as in his, a place where Christ's power is at rest.

crossReferences.note: Isaiah sees the Lord enthroned and cries out that he is ruined. The great vision of God produces awareness of weakness, not pride. Paul's vision and thorn belong to the same pattern, in which seeing the glory of God is followed by a humbling that keeps the servant low.

The nations left in the land would be barbs in the eyes and thorns in the sides of Israel. The Greek Old Testament uses the same noun that Paul uses for his thorn, and the passage shows thorns standing for persistent harassment, which is why many think the thorn was opposition.

The LORD permits Satan to afflict Job but sets a limit. Satan can act only as far as God allows. This is the pattern behind Paul's thorn: a messenger of Satan whose work is bounded and turned to God's purpose of keeping His servant humble.

Satan asked to sift Simon like wheat, and Jesus prayed that his faith would not fail. The enemy's attack and the Lord's care run side by side, and the end is strengthening. It parallels Paul's thorn and the Lord's promise of sufficient grace.

Jesus prays three times that the cup may pass if it is possible, and the answer is strength to drink it. The three pleas of 2 Corinthians 12:8 echo the pattern of Gethsemane, where the servant asks honestly and is answered by grace and not by removal.

Paul says he first preached to the Galatians because of an illness, and that they would have torn out their eyes for him. It is the main text cited for a bodily thorn, but it does not name the thorn of 2 Corinthians 12, and the connection remains a possibility rather than a certainty.

Christ was crucified in weakness yet lives by God's power, and we are weak in Him yet live with Him by God's power. This gives the christological ground of 12:9 and 12:10: the pattern of weakness and power is not an idea but the shape of the cross and the resurrection.

The weakness of God is stronger than man's strength, and God chose the weak things of the world to shame the strong. Paul's boast in weakness applies this earlier teaching to his own life and shows that it is the consistent logic of the gospel.

We have a high priest who sympathises with our weaknesses and a throne of grace where we receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need. It is the New Testament statement of what Paul experienced: the Lord does not remove every weakness but meets us in it with grace.

The LORD gives power to the faint and increases the strength of the weak. It is the Old Testament form of the principle in the Lord's answer to Paul, and shows that perfected power in weakness is not a new idea but the way God has always acted.

The God of all comfort comforts us in all our troubles. The verb that appears as 'comfort' here is the same word Paul uses for his plea in 12:8. The answer is not removal but comfort in the deeper sense of strengthening grace.

study.oneStory:
The Bible opens with a garden and humans walking with God, and the deepest loss of the fall is the loss of that nearness. Paul's journey to Paradise is a rare glimpse of that garden restored, and the Bible's last chapters show it in full, where the tree of life stands in the Paradise of God, Revelation 2:7, and the river flows from the throne, Revelation 22:1 to 2. This passage gives a small preview of the ending, and Paul says it was too holy to describe.

But the story does not go to the garden without passing through weakness. From Abraham's barren wife to Gideon's reduced army, from the exile to the manger, God chooses the weak, and the great reversal is the cross, where the Son of God was crucified in weakness. The resurrection is the vindication of that way. The Lord's answer to Paul, 'My power is perfected in weakness,' is a summary of how the whole Bible works.

The passage also touches the great conflict between God and the enemy. In Genesis 3, a serpent speaks, and the woman and man are led away from trust. In Job 2, Satan acts under limits. In the Gospels, Satan sifts Peter and tempts Jesus. In this letter he is the god of this age who blinds minds, 4:4, and the messenger who buffets Paul. The story always shows him bounded, and what he means for harm God turns to good, so that even the thorn becomes a place where Christ's grace is proved sufficient.

The church lives in the middle of this. Believers have been given the Spirit as a pledge, and they know the power of Christ, but they still carry a treasure in jars of clay, 4:7. They pray and are sometimes answered with grace and not removal. The promise of the passage is that this is not a failure but a stage on the way.

And it ends in the new creation, where weakness is finished. Paul says in 1 Corinthians 15:43 that what is sown in weakness is raised in power, and in Romans 8:18 that present sufferings are not comparable to the glory to come. The one who was caught up for a moment will be with the Lord forever, 1 Thessalonians 4:17, and no thorn will remain, since there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain, Revelation 21:4.

quiz.q: Why does Paul tell of the vision in the third person and refuse to boast in it?

options.text: So that no one will credit him beyond what they see, and he can boast only in his weaknesses.
options.note: Verses 5 and 6 make this his stated aim.

options.text: Because he is not sure the vision really happened.
options.note: He is certain of the vision; his reticence is deliberate humility, not doubt.

options.text: Because he was forbidden to speak of it at all.
options.note: He was not permitted to repeat what he heard, but he does report that he was caught up.

options.text: Because visions do not matter to the Christian life.
options.note: The point is not that revelation is worthless but that Paul refuses to trade on it.

quiz.q: What was the purpose of the thorn in the flesh?

options.text: To keep Paul from becoming conceited over the surpassing revelations.
options.note: Verse 7 states the reason twice, framing the thorn.

options.text: To punish Paul for a hidden sin.
options.note: The thorn is preventive and humbling, not punitive.

options.text: To prove that Satan is stronger than God.
options.note: Though a messenger of Satan, the thorn serves God's good purpose.

options.text: To show that Paul lacked enough faith to be healed.
options.note: The unremoved thorn displays grace, not a failure of faith.

quiz.q: How did the Lord answer Paul's threefold plea?

options.text: My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness.
options.note: Verse 9 gives the Lord's own words, the heart of the passage.

options.text: He removed the thorn after the third request.
options.note: The Lord did not remove it; He gave sufficient grace instead.

options.text: He promised to explain the reason later.
options.note: The answer was grace to bear it, not a deferred explanation.

options.text: He rebuked Paul for asking at all.
options.note: The Lord answers tenderly with sufficient grace, not rebuke.

quiz.q: Why does Paul now delight in weakness?

options.text: Because when he is weak the power of Christ rests on him, so that when he is weak, then he is strong.
options.note: Verses 9 and 10 draw out the paradox.

options.text: Because weakness earns extra merit with God.
options.note: It is not merit but the resting of Christ's power that makes weakness a boast.

options.text: Because he enjoys suffering for its own sake.
options.note: He delights in weakness for the sake of Christ and His power, not suffering itself.

options.text: Because weakness proves God has abandoned him.
options.note: Weakness is exactly where God's power draws near, not a sign of abandonment.

questions: Paul had an experience most would boast about for a lifetime, yet he refused to trade on it. What spiritual highs or credentials are you tempted to lean on instead of resting in Christ's grace?
God gave a thorn to keep Paul humble. Can you see ways God has used an unwelcome trouble to guard you from pride or to draw you closer to Himself?
Three times Paul pleaded and the answer was grace rather than removal. How does it change your prayers to know that sufficient grace, not the removal of every trouble, may be God's best answer?
The Lord says His power is perfected in weakness. Where do you most feel your weakness right now, and what would it look like to invite Christ's power to rest there?
Paul learned to say, when I am weak, then I am strong. What would need to change in you to begin boasting in weakness rather than hiding it?

translationNotes.note: The parenthetical whether in the body or out of it I do not know, but God knows keeps Paul's careful uncertainty about the manner of the vision.

The BSB footnote observes that some translators end the previous sentence after verse 6 and begin verse 7 with So to keep me from becoming conceited because of these surpassingly great revelations; either way the revelations are the reason the thorn was given.
Perfected renders teleioo, to bring to completion or full expression; the Lord's power is not merely present in weakness but brought to its fullest display there.
